Dear Secretary Reese:

        In response to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) May 22, 2026,
deficiency letter and request for additional information issued in the above-captioned proceeding
(“Deficiency Letter”),1 Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc. (“Tri-State”) submits
this response and accompanying attachments (collectively, “Deficiency Response”). Narrative
responses to the Commission’s questions are included in Attachment A. Furthermore, as discussed
below, Tri-State also submits under Attachment 2 a proposed alternative Western HILT/HILA for
filing on compliance (“Alternative Western HILT/HILA”).

        For the reasons explained below, Tri-State respectfully requests that the Commission establish
a shortened comment period of no more than ten (10) days for this Response. Tri-State further requests
the Commission act expeditiously to issue an order accepting Tri-State’s proposed HILT Filing,2
including the HILT, and pro forma HILA, or, if necessary, the Alternative Western HILT/HILA, with

I.         BACKGROUND

        On March 26, 2026, pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and Part 35 of
the Commission’s regulations, Tri-State submitted the HILT Filing.3 The HILT Filing included the
HILT and a pro forma HILA. As explained in the Transmittal Letter, Tri-State’s proposed HIL
Program is intended to establish a biennial process in which Tri-State objectively evaluates all HILs,
defined as loads 45 MW or above or loads forecast to exceed 45 MW in four years, seeking to
interconnect to anywhere within Tri-State’s system to ensure there are no adverse impacts to Tri-
State’s Utility Members and the Utility Members can, in turn, offer large loads a transparent and
settled process for establishing service.4

        On April 16, 2026, Wheat Belt Public Power District (“Wheat Belt”), the Data Center Coalition
(“DCC”), and Poudre Valley Rural Electric Association, Inc. (“Poudre Valley”) filed comments
addressing various aspects of the HILT Filing. On May 6, 2026, Tri-State filed a Motion for Leave to
Answer and Answer (“Answer”) in response.5 Amongst other things, the Answer addressed comments
regarding Tri-State’s obligations to serve all of its Utility Members’ requirements under their
respective Wholesale Electric Service Contracts (“WESCs”)6 and treatment of Eastern and Western
Utility Members. For example, the Answer addressed how Tri-State is proposing to implement the
HILT with respect to its Eastern Interconnection Utility Members if Basin Electric Power Cooperative
(“Basin”) establishes different requirements for its own large load tariff, e.g., imposing a lower MW
threshold.7 Tri-State filed a subsequent Answer on May 18, 2026, in response to additional comments
from High Plains Power, Inc. (“May 18 Answer”),8 which reiterated that the HILT does not redefine
Tri-State’s service commitments as contemplated in the WESCs because the HILT does not diminish
Tri-State’s service obligation.9

       On May 22, 2026, the Commission issued the Deficiency Letter seeking additional information
and responses to questions regarding, inter alia, Tri-State’s obligations under its WESC with Basin,

II.        PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE WESTERN HILT/HILA

         In addition to the HILT and pro forma HILA submitted for filing with the March 26 HILT
Filing, Tri-State submits herein as Attachment 2 a proposed Alternative Western HILT and pro forma
HILA. The Alternative Western HILT would limit the HILT program’s scope to Utility Members’
loads in the Western Interconnection. Utility Members that sought service for large loads in the Eastern
Interconnection would not proceed under the Western HILT. Instead, Tri-State, the Utility Member,
and the wholesale service provider Tri-State has contracted with to serve Utility Member load in the
Eastern Interconnection, Basin, would confer to determine if modifications to the standard Western
HILT and/or pro forma HILA would be required to meet specific service requirements from Basin.
Tri-State would then make a filing with the Commission of the agreements reflecting terms and
conditions that would meet the particular service requirements that Basin may demand and which
would otherwise be just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Attachment 3
contains a PDF redline showing potential change s to the Alternative Western HILT marked against
the initial HILT and pro forma HILA for filing on compliance if the Commission instead determines it
is appropriate.

        While Tri-State believes that its Deficiency Response demonstrates that the initial HILT and
pro forma HILA are just and reasonable, if the Commission determines, after review of the narrative
responses, that it cannot accept the HILT Filing due to remaining concerns with disparate treatment of
Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection and Western Interconnection loads, Tri-State
respectfully requests that the Commission accept the filing, subject to compliance to file the proposed
Alternative Western HILT. The Alternative Western HILT is to be filed as Rate Schedule No. 435,
effective as of July 16, 2026, thirty (30) days from filing, or the same effective date proposed for the
HILT and pro forma HILA, or as soon thereafter as the Commission finds appropriate.

           A.       Description of Alternative Western HILT

        The revisions made in the Alternative Western HILT and pro forma HILA are intended only to
remove language describing the application of the HIL Program to Tri-State’s Utility Members’
Eastern Interconnection HILs. For example, Section 1 of the HILT is revised to apply only to HILs
located in the Western Interconnection,10 and the Definitions and Acronyms in Section 2 are revised to
add new defined terms for Eastern Interconnection and Western Interconnection. Further, the
definitions for High Impact Load and High Impact Load Project are revised to refer specifically to a

load addition located in the Western Interconnection that meets the applicable requirements.11 Also,
Section 3 is revised to remove Section 3.6, which refers to Basin’s development of a large load tariff,
as Basin’s large load tariff does not affect Tri-State’s Western Utility Members.12

        The Alternative Western HILA would contain conforming changes, including deletion of
Basin-related defined terms in Section 1- Definitions, deletion of the defined term “Security DUE
Notice – EI” (and conforming revision to remove that defined term in the definition of “Security Due
Notice.”13 Accordingly, Section 3.G and Section 4.B of the Western HILA are revised to remove
language addressing obligations associated with the Security Due Notice – EI and the Eastern
Interconnection.14 Similar revisions in Section 7 remove references to Eastern Interconnection Security
obligations.15 Finally, former Section 10.C.1.d that referred to the ability for Utility Members’ Eastern
Interconnection HILs to participate in a Basin large load tariff program would be deleted because it is
no longer needed for the Western HILA.16 These changes do not substantively impact, revise, affect or
otherwise change the terms and conditions of Tri-State’s Western Interconnection Utility Members
participation in Tri-State’s HILA Program.

        To the extent necessary, Tri-State respectfully requests that the Commission waive any filing
requirements contained in 18 C.F.R. Part 35 with respect to the Alternative Western HILT/HILA that
are not met or addressed by this filing or the March 26 HILT Filing. Good cause exists for such
waiver. This Deficiency Response merely clarifies the existing record from Tri-State’s HILT Filing
and does not include any new information not already provided with the Transmittal Letter to the HILT
Filing; therefore, it substantially complies with the requirements of Part 35 of the Commission’s rules
and regulations applicable to filings of this type. Tri-State requests a waiver of any applicable
requirement of Part 35 for which a waiver is not specifically requested, if necessary, to permit the
Alternative Western HILA/HILT to become effective along with the HILT and pro forma HILA as
proposed.

           B.       Both the HILT and Alternative Western HILT are Just and Reasonable and
                    Not Unduly Discriminatory or Preferential
       As Tri-State demonstrated in its HILT Filing, the HILT and pro forma HILA are just and
reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. The HIL Program is consistent with

Commission policy governing transmission service requests, transmission planning, and cost causation
principles.17 The HIL Program is designed to treat Tri-State’s Utility Members serving HILs in the
Eastern and Western interconnection consistently, acknowledging that Basin may seek to impose
additional or different requirements to address issues that exist only in the Eastern Interconnection and
pursuant to its service obligations under the Tri-State/Basin wholesale power contract.

        As discussed below and in the narrative response under Attachment 1, Tri-State commits to
filing any such differences related to Utility Member Eastern Interconnection HIL with the
Commission for review, which will ensure any different terms are the result of legitimate conditions of
service and, therefore, just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Because Tri-
State’s Utility Members Eastern Interconnection loads are served through a wholesale power contract
between Tri-State and Basin, they are not similarly situated to Tri-State’s Utility Members Western
Interconnection loads, which instead are served by Tri-State through a Colorado Public Utility
Commission-regulated resource acquisition process.18

        Tri-State may face the imposition from Basin of an additional set of service requirements for its
Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection HILs. A distinct set of risks exists for Tri-State’s Utility
Members’ Western Interconnection HILs. Alternatively, Basin may impose less stringent
requirements, in which case Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection loads should realize
the benefit of such requirements. Or, in all likelihood, Basin could impose a mixture of the two.
Moreover, because the terms of service Basin could seek to impose on Tri-State to serve HILs under
the Basin wholesale power contract are not set out in a program required by Basin to be filed with the
Commission, or any State utility commission, Tri-State’s must take a flexible approach to
appropriately reflect such hypothetical terms within the proposed pro forma HILA and proposed HILT
without being overly speculative.

        These differences between how Tri-State’s Utility Members are served justify the allowance
that Tri-State created for deviations from the pro forma HILA to accommodate conditions that Basin
may impose. The potential for non-conforming HILAs for Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern
Interconnection HILs to include service requirements imposed by a Basin large load program do not
support a finding that the HILT is unduly discriminatory because Tri-State’s Utility Members are not
similarly situated when it comes to resource supply.19 To the extent there were separate requirements,
Tri-State would be obligated to explain the differences in a non-conforming HILA filed to meet

        Notwithstanding the foregoing, Tri-State proposes the attached Alternative Western HILT as an

        This alternative tariff is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory for three reasons
beyond those set forth for the original HILT in the HILT Filing, and the Commission could instead
accept the Tri-State’s filing with the same effective date, subject to the condition that Tri-State submit

        First, Tri-State has not received any Member Project Requests for the HILs located in the
Eastern Interconnection, while Tri-State has received 40 Member Project Requests for HILs located in

standard effective date 60 days after the date of filing, it is too late to submit additional Member
Project Requests for the current HIL Cycle. This means that no Utility Member or HIL would suffer
discriminatory or preferential harm from the alternative proposal until the next HIL Cycle begins in
approximately two years, which provides Tri-State, Basin, Eastern Utility Members and the
Commission additional time to resolve the issue without harm to Eastern Utility Members.

        Second, with one limited exception,25 all of Tri-State’s Utility Members with load in the
Eastern Interconnection served by Basin have served Tri-State with unconditional notices to withdraw

states that the Initial Term of the agreement “will be for a minimum of fifteen (15) years after the
Operation Date, and the Initial Term may not extend beyond the term of the WESC.”26 Moreover, the
pro forma HILA provides that, “Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, this
Agreement will terminate concurrently with the termination of the WESC.”27 This means that these
members, including Wheatbelt, have chosen to terminate their WESCs within two years, and, thus,
there remains only one Utility Member with a small portion of Eastern Interconnection load28 that
satisfies the concomitant HILA requirements for a minimum fifteen-year initial term that does not
extend beyond the term of a members’ WESC.29 Accordingly, there is no current need for an Eastern
HILT and there may not ever be a need for an Eastern HILT, with the remaining Eastern
Interconnection load representing approximately 2% of Tri-State’s total load.

        Third, should a Utility Member’s Eastern Interconnection load become eligible to satisfy the
minimum term requirement, or should HEA submit an Member Project Request for a HIL in the
Eastern Interconnection, Tri-State will commit to filing, on an ad hoc basis, comparable member-
specific tariffs until such time as it can propose a generally applicable tariff for Utility Members’
Eastern Interconnection loads that captures Basin’s large load tariff requirements, if any, that are just,
reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. If Basin has not imposed terms that are
inconsistent with the HILT, the ad hoc member-specific filings will be consistent with the HILT and
pro forma HILA. If Basin has imposed different terms, and such terms are just, reasonable, and not
unduly discriminatory or preferential, the ad hoc member-specific filings will reflect those terms, and
the Commission may then evaluate the member-specific HILTs and HILAs de novo. Such a result
would be an improvement from the status quo ex ante. Tri-State is authorized to represent that HEA,
the sole member with Eastern Interconnection load that has not submitted an unconditional notice of
withdrawal, does not oppose Tri-State's HILT filing or its proposal for an Alternative Western

V.      REQUEST FOR SHORTENED COMMENT PERIOD AND EXPEDITED
        CONSIDERATION
       Given the urgent need to interconnect data centers and other large loads,30 Tri-State respectfully
requests that the Commission establish a shortened comment period of no more than (10) days for this
Response.

        Additionally, Tri-State requests the Commission act on the HILT Filing as expeditiously as
possible. Expedited Commission action and issuance of an order on this matter with the requested
effective date of the HILT on this matter is warranted so that Tri-State can serve HILs as quickly as
possible.31 Furthermore, expedited Commission action will provide commercial certainty to Tri-State’s

VI.        EFFECTIVE DATE

        Given Tri-State’s urgent need to provide a reasoned, objective and transparent large load
program to its Utility Members, which are facing unprecedented demands from HILs, and to
interconnect data centers and other large loads without undue delay,32 Tri-State’s requests that the
Commission act expeditiously to issue an order and grant an effective date of July 16, 2026, thirty (30)
days from filing for the HILT and pro forma HILA, or as soon thereafter as the Commission finds
appropriate, and the same effective date to the extent that the Commission instead requires a
compliance filing for the proposed Alternative Western HILT/HILA, as discussed above. Tri-State
submits that it has provided sufficient evidentiary support to enable the Commission to accept the
proposed HILT, pro forma HILA, and Alternative Western HILT/HILA, as just and reasonable to be
effective as requested.33

VII.       CONCLUSION

       For the reasons set forth above, in the Transmittal Letter, Answer, and in the attached narrative
response, Tri-State reiterates its request that the Commission approve the HILT Filing, including the
HILT, pro forma HILA, or the Alternative Western HILT/HILA, without condition or delay, effective
July 16, 2026, thirty (30) days from filing, as requested, or as soon thereafter as the Commission finds
appropriate, establish a shortened comment period of no more than ten (10) days, and grant Tri-State
any other waivers or relief the Commission deems necessary to effectuate the foregoing.

               Attachment 1 – Narrative Responses to Deficiency Letter Questions

        Tri-State’s responses to the Commission’s Deficiency Letter are below. Capitalized terms
not defined herein have the same meaning as in the HILT Filing.

Commission Request No. 1

1. In your transmittal, you state that “Tri-State serves its Utility Members in the Eastern
   Interconnection through a Wholesale Power Contract with Basin Electric Power
   Cooperative (Basin). It is Tri-State’s understanding that Basin has developed its own
   program to serve large loads, which could be applicable to large load requests located in the
   Eastern Interconnection.” Additionally, in your answer, you state that “Tri-State has
   provided a pro forma HILA as part of the HILT Filing to put all Utility Members on notice
   that Basin could have separate requirements.”

         a. Please explain why the Wholesale Power Contract requires Tri-State’s Utility
            Members to meet any and all obligations from Basin. Please explain why these
            obligations are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

Tri-State Response:

        Tri-State has entered into the Wholesale Power Contract with Basin to serve the vast
majority of Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection member load (the “Basin WPC”). 1 The Basin WPC
does not require Tri-State’s Utility Members to meet any and all obligations from Basin. Tri-State
and Basin, as the parties to the Basin WPC, fulfill the obligations and receive the benefits of the
contract in accordance with its terms and conditions. However, the Basin WPC does raise the
possibility that the terms under which Tri-State serves its members in the Eastern Interconnection,
and accordingly the risks, could be different from those in the Western Interconnection. 2

       Basin does not currently and may never implement a formal standardized large load tariff
or program that uniformly impacts service conditions for any Tri-State Utility Members served by



1
         Basin Electric Power Cooperative, Rate Schedules, Rate Schedule No. 16A (Tri-State G & T Association,
Inc. - East) (0.0.0).
2
          Basin Elec. Power Coop., 172 FERC ¶ 61,221 (2020) (order accepting under section 205 of the FPA and
instituting an investigation under section 206 of the FPA Basin’s filing of Basin Rate Schedules Nos 1-19, i.e., long-
term Wholesale Power Contracts). The Commission has since accepted Basin’s notices of cancellation with respect to
the long-term Wholesale Power Contracts with its members effective July 16, 2025, finding that Basin was no longer
a public utility as defined under section 201 of the FPA. Basin Elec. Power Cooperative, 192 FERC ¶ 61,218 at P 17
(2025), order on reh’g and clarification, 195 FERC ¶ 61,017 at P 23 (2026) (“Basin was a Commission-jurisdictional
entity with its rates on file with the Commission during the locked-in period and therefore the Commission must
ensure that jurisdictional rates charged to customers were just and reasonable.”).
                                                  Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.
                                                                                        ER26-1929-___
                                                                             Deficiency Letter Response

Basin in the Eastern Interconnection. 3 Furthermore, if terms imposed by Basin on Tri-State’s
Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection Basin loads differ from the HILT terms applied to Tri-
State’s Western Utility Members, for example, a different minimum threshold for a High Impact
Load (“HIL”) customer, that difference alone would not cause the HILA to be unjust and
unreasonable or result in undue discrimination or preferential treatment. 4 Because Basin has yet
to implement a standardized large load tariff or program with respect to Tri-State’s Utility
Members’ Eastern Interconnection Basin loads, and grants its board final discretion to approve
service terms for large loads, any analysis of whether any hypothetical terms or conditions imposed
by Basin are just and reasonable is speculative and it would be premature for Tri-State to make
such a demonstration. It is Tri-State’s understanding that Basin has designed a flexible framework
for serving large loads, which could result in different programmatic requirements for each HIL.
That said, a fundamental precept of the Commission’s just and reasonable policy is that there is no
one just and reasonable rate. 5 There exists a zone of reasonableness within which rate terms may
be found to be just and reasonable. To the extent that any terms imposed by Basin differ from those
proposed by Tri-State, those terms may also be just and reasonable. If they are not, they will not
be imposed on the Utility Members, either because Tri-State would not consent to include them as
part of Basin’s HIL service in the Eastern Interconnection or they would be subject to Commission
oversight through the eventual filing Tri-State will be obligated to make.

        Similarly, the application of different terms to Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern and
Western Interconnection loads does not create undue discrimination or preferential treatment.
FERC has already recognized the differences between serving Tri-State’s Utility Members’
Eastern and Western Interconnection loads, and found that differing treatment of Utility Members
based on the cost structure of resources serving a load location can be just and reasonable and not
unduly discriminatory or preferential. 6 FERC found that Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern and
Western Interconnection loads are not similarly situated, which justified the implementation of a
different contract termination payment calculation methodology for Tri-State’s Utility Members’
Eastern Interconnection loads compared to Western Interconnection loads. The differences in the
CTP Proceeding were driven by the Commission’s conclusion that Tri-State’s prudently chosen
resource to meet its service obligations in the Eastern Interconnection, the Basin WPC, required a

3
         The load of Tri-State’s Eastern Utility Members is almost exclusively served by Basin, but there is a single
delivery point in New Mexico served through an alternative provider. Accordingly, this response will refer to loads
affected by Basin’s service requirements as Basin Eastern Interconnection Loads.
4
        FERC has recognized that discrimination or preference for Eastern and Western members is allowed, i.e.
CTP, BYOR (Eastern members have to bring their resources in the West) owing to the resource planning and
investment risk differences between regions.
5
         See, e.g., Cities of Bethany v. FERC, 727 F.2d 1131, 1136 (D.C. Cir. 1984) (when determining whether a rate
was just and reasonable, the Commission properly did not consider “whether a proposed rate schedule is more or less
reasonable than alternative rate designs”).
6
         See generally, Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc., 185 FERC ¶ 61,201 at P 574 (2023),
order on reh’g 185 FERC ¶ 61,201 (2024) (“CTP Order on ID”).
                                                  Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.
                                                                                        ER26-1929-___
                                                                             Deficiency Letter Response

different CTP methodology. The Commission required the establishment of a CTP method and
terms for the Eastern Interconnection that accounted for the Basin WPC’s specific terms and
conditions. Similarly, the Commission has approved distinct treatment for Utility Members in the
Eastern Interconnection under Tri-State’s Bring Your Own Resource (“BYOR”) Tariff. 7
Moreover, in the BYOR Tariff, the Commission specifically accepted Tri-State’s ability to “flow
through” the requirements of Basin’s high impact load tariffs. It would be arbitrary and capricious
for the Commission not to accept the same treatment here. The HILT’s treatment of Tri-State’s
Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection Basin loads follows the Commission’s directives related
to the Basin WPC and the different service conditions that exist within the two interconnections,
such as the different financial risk and debt that Tri-State undertakes in the Western
Interconnection.

        Here, Basin may seek to impose terms on Tri-State in connection with the service Tri-State
provides to its Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection Basin loads. The HILT is designed to
accommodate such terms, so long as they are just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or
preferential. The Commission has explained that “the FPA does not prohibit all discrimination,
only undue discrimination. In general, discrimination is ‘undue’ when there is a difference of rates,
terms or conditions among similarly situated customers.” 8 Here, different treatment between
Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection Basin load and Western Interconnection load is not
“undue discrimination” because the Commission has already found that Tri-State’s Eastern
Interconnection Utility Members and Western Interconnection Utility Members are not similarly
situated, and the HILT, as a risk management / risk mitigation tool will appropriately account for
differing risks posed by members that are not similarly situated. For example, the HILT and pro
forma HILA help mitigate risk from potential stranded resources and aid compliance with resource
acquisition processes under Tri-State’s state-regulated resource planning requirements for serving
Utility Member Western Interconnection load, which are issues that Tri-State does not directly face
for load served in the Eastern Interconnection by Basin. Moreover, the proposed HILT is designed
to provide the flexibility necessary to address any future differences, when they occur, in a
proceeding where the non-conforming HILA is filed with the Commission for approval.

It is Tri-State’s intention that any material term or condition that Basin imposes on HILs in the
Eastern Interconnection that affects Tri-State’s ability to serve its Utility Members’ Eastern
Interconnection HIL would be incorporated in non-conforming Eastern HILAs. Importantly, as
discussed above, Tri-State would make a filing of the nonconforming HILA with FERC that
identifies the terms that deviate from the pro forma HILA. At the time of filing, Tri-State would
make the requisite demonstration that such terms are just and reasonable. At that point, the issue

7
         BYOR Tariff, Rate Schedule No. 371 (1.0.0), at 4.4.6.2. (“All HIL BYOR Projects proposed by Tri-State
Utility Members located in the Eastern Interconnection must also be located in the Eastern Interconnection, and must
follow any high impact load processes, tariffs, or requirements of Basin Electric Power Cooperative.”).
8
        Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 116 FERC ¶ 61,274, at P 207 (2006), on reh’g, 119 FERC ¶ 61,076, at P
369 (2007).
                                                   Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.
                                                                                         ER26-1929-___
                                                                              Deficiency Letter Response

of whether specific terms and conditions that Basin may require for Utility Member Eastern
Interconnection loads will be ripe for Commission review.

        It is also important to note that Tri-State cannot currently identify what terms Basin may
seek to impose that would deviate from those in the HILT and HILAs. Should Basin impose terms
of service for HILs, Basin is no longer subject to FERC’s public utility jurisdiction, which would
prevent modification of those terms in a FERC proceeding. 9 Accordingly, while any terms Basin
could seek to impose must first comply with Basin’s contractual obligations to Tri-State pursuant
to the Basin WPC, the Commission should consider any contractually compliant terms or
conditions imposed by Basin that are passed through to Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern
Interconnection HILs in a nonconforming HILA to be de jure just and reasonable, as they are
outside the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction or regulatory authority. 10 In the Prior HILT
Order, the Commission rejected that proposed HILT because it threatened to impermissibly
interfere with rates that are outside the Commission’s jurisdiction. 11 Although the concern there
was the perceived interference with, and potential indirect regulation of, non-jurisdictional retail
rates, the same principle applies here with Basin’s wholesale rates. Preventing Tri-State from
passing through a term that is imposed on it by Basin’s non-jurisdictional wholesale service, or
modifying such term, would be the functional equivalent of indirectly regulating the terms and
conditions of Basin’s non-jurisdictional wholesale service.




9
         See infra note 2.
10
        Nonetheless, Tri-State’s position in negotiating agreements with Basin will be to use any flexibility provided
under Basin’s large load program to develop terms and conditions appropriate for Tri-State to meet its obligation to
have such non-conforming HILAs approved by the Commission.
11
         See Prior HILT Order at P 49.
                                          Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.
                                                                                ER26-1929-___
                                                                     Deficiency Letter Response

Commission Request No. 2

2. In your answer, you state that “to the extent that Basin imposes additional, separate
   requirements outside of the HILT through Basin’s own large load program, the HILT
   acknowledges that, as a contractual matter, Eastern Utility Members may also need to
   comply with those requirements. It may be the case that Tri-State would need to make a
   future filing at FERC memorializing any requirements that Basin will require of Tri-State’s
   Eastern Utility Members when it becomes clear those will apply. But it is also possible that
   there may not be a need for a separate filing.”

       a. Please explain how Tri-State will determine whether a future Commission filing
          will be necessary.

Tri-State Response:

        Under any circumstance where Basin was not willing, or not able, to serve a Tri-State
Eastern Utility Member High-Impact Load on terms materially consistent with Tri-State’s pro
forma HILA, then a Commission filing would be necessary for a non-conforming HILA. The only
circumstance where a filing may not be necessary is where Basin proposes to impose a less
stringent requirement than that proposed by Tri-State in the pro forma HILA, but the Eastern
Utility Member voluntarily chooses to abide by the standard requirement set forth in the pro forma
HILA.

        Should the Commission accept the Tri-State Alternative Western HILT/HILA, described
in the transmittal letter, Tri-State would need to file an Eastern HILT if and when it and Basin
agreed to a binding, generally applicable HILT approach for Tri-State’s Eastern Utility Members.

       b. To the extent Basin proposes to impose terms and conditions on Eastern Utility
          Members, please explain whether Tri-State would specify those terms and
          conditions in its tariff through a future filing under section 205 of the Federal
          Power Act.

Tri-State Response:

       As discussed above, any terms Basin imposes on Tri-State that are inconsistent with those
contained in the pro forma HILA will prompt the filing of a non-conforming HILA in which Tri-
State would describe all non-conforming terms and provide the detail necessary for the
Commission to evaluate the justness and reasonableness of the non-conforming terms prior to
becoming effective.

       Alternatively, if FERC were to accept the Alternative Western HILT/HILA, Tri-State
would need to file an Eastern HILT once it agreed with Basin on a generally applicable HILT
approach for Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection HILs.
                                          Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.
                                                                                ER26-1929-___
                                                                     Deficiency Letter Response

       c. Please explain whether the provisions relating to Eastern Utility Members are
          intended to incorporate by reference any current or future requirement
          promulgated by Basin.

Tri-State Response:

       No. Any requirement or non-conforming term that Basin places on Tri-State in its effort to
serve a Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection HIL request would be included in a non-
conforming HILA filing with the Commission or would eventually be included in an Eastern HILT
or HILA if the Commission accepts the alternative Western HILT.
                                                   Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.
                                                                                         ER26-1929-___
                                                                              Deficiency Letter Response

Commission Request No. 3

3. Section 7.B of the HIL Agreement provides that, “if the load of the Project is located in the
   Eastern Interconnection and served pursuant to the Basin East Wholesale Power Contract,
   the Security Amount will be the amount of the Basin Security.” Section 1 of the HIL
   Agreement defines Basin Security as “any maximum security, collateral, or other financial
   commitment that Tri-State may be required to provide to Basin related to the Project
   pursuant to any Basin-required tariff, policy, procedure, or process.”

         a. Please explain whether the amount of the Basin Security is limited or constrained
            by any of the terms and conditions of the HIL Tariff.

Tri-State Response:

        No, the Basin Security is not constrained by any of the terms and conditions of the HILT.
Tri-State would require the exact amount of security from an Eastern Utility Member that Basin
would require of Tri-State, without any additional markup or an administrative fee. If the Basin
Security amount were an amount less than Tri-State’s security, the Utility Member would pay the
lower amount. Because security under the HILT is intended to protect Tri-State’s other Utility
Members from cost shifts, it is appropriate that the Utility Member is only responsible for paying
the security amount required of Tri-State, which avoids cross-subsidization and is consistent with
the general principle of cost causation. With respect to security, the cost imposed would be the
security amount assessed by Basin and payment of such amount would mitigate any cross-
subsidization risk. Furthermore, it would not be appropriate to require the standard $1.87 million
security amount for Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern Interconnection Basin loads if that
amount does not accurately and reasonably reflect the costs and risks they imposed on the Tri-
State system. 12 As noted, the issue of whether a specific security amount Basin may require is just
and reasonable is not currently ripe for Commission review because no security amount has been
proposed.

         b. Please explain how the Basin Security would be implemented. For example, please
            explain whether Tri-State would give notice of the Basin Security to the Eastern
            Utility Member prior to execution of the HIL Agreement.




12
         The beneficiary pays and cost-causation principle requires costs to be allocated to those who cause the costs
to be incurred and to those that enjoy the resulting benefits. S.C. Pub. Serv. Auth. v. FERC, 762 F.3d 41, 87 (D.C. Cir.
2014) (citing Nat’l Ass’n of Regul. Util. Comm’rs v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277, 1285 (D.C. Cir. 2007)).
                                           Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc.
                                                                                 ER26-1929-___
                                                                      Deficiency Letter Response

Tri-State Response:
        Tri-State would promptly notify an Eastern Utility Member upon receipt of Basin’s
security requirements in advance of a filing of a non-conforming HILA. The specific timing of
notice of the security amount, or the formula to calculate such amount, and the security due date
could be affected by Basin processes, but in both cases, notice would be provided prior to either
execution or filing of the non-conforming HILA. Such filing would then provide the Commission
with the opportunity to evaluate all proposed security procedures to ensure the agreement provided
sufficient advance notice to the affected Tri-State Utility Member through the non-conforming
HILA, an Eastern HILT, or an ad hoc member-specific HILT.
       Importantly, under the filed-rate doctrine, Tri-State would be barred from requiring
payment from a Utility Member for a security amount that was not previously authorized by the
Commission, whether under the pro forma HILA, a non-conforming HILA, or the filing of an
Eastern HILT or ad hoc member-specific HILT.
       c. Please explain whether the Eastern Utility Member would be subject to additional
          financial commitments after the execution of a HIL Agreement to the extent Basin
          modified its security requirements.

Tri-State Response:

        As a starting point, Tri-State would seek to enter into an agreement that defines and
describes all security requirements and procedures, and financial conditions material to the HILT,
at a level sufficient for inclusion in subsequent HILT or HILA filings, that would be made prior to
any notification of or request for security from an Utility Member’s Eastern Interconnection HIL
through a binding contract with Basin not susceptible to subsequent modification.

        To date, neither Tri-State nor Basin have engaged in negotiations for such an agreement,
and Tri-State does not have access to, or opportunity to review, any Basin HIL service agreements.
Tri-State has no information regarding whether Basin plans to include security provisions in a
future tariff or adopt or revise any Board Policies that may impact the security amount.
Notwithstanding any uncertainty regarding Basin’s future plans, as discussed above, Tri-State will
include any modifications to the security amount in the pro forma HILA, a non-conforming HILA,
or the filing of an Eastern HILT, or ad hoc member-specific HILT for submission to the
Commission.

                   TRI-STATE GENERATION AND TRANSMISSION ASSOCIATION, INC…/
                          HIGH IMPACT LOAD PROGRAM TARIFF (“TARIFF”)

   I.      APPLICABILITY, PURPOSE, AND OVERVIEW

This Tariﬀ sets forth the procedures, terms, and conditions governing the High Impact Load Program
(“Program”).

   1.1.   Applicability. The Program is available to all Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association,
          Inc. (“Tri-State”) Utility Member loads located in the Western Interconnection.

   1.2.   Purpose. To establish a fair, repeatable method for integrating High Impact Loads onto the Tri-
          State system without adverse impacts to reliability, aﬀordability, or responsibility in Tri-State’s
          provision of electric service to its Utility Members.

   1.3.   Overview. Tri-State has a robust annual load forecast process that includes Utility Member
          input aimed at forecasting resource needs over the term of the Wholesale Electric Service
          Contract (“WESC”). Tri-State includes the impacts of legislative, regulatory, and industry
          initiatives across its territory in the load forecasting process, to the extent known and
          quantiﬁable. Moreover, Tri-State is resource-regulated by the Colorado Public Utilities
          Commission. Outside of Tri-State’s routine load forecasting and planning processes, which
          capture the addition or expansion of certain Utility Member loads, High Impact Loads will have
          signiﬁcant impacts to resource and transmission planning processes and related reliability,
          aﬀordability, and responsibility metrics. To ensure that all planning metrics can be successfully
          met, Tri-State is establishing a threshold at which a Utility Member-requested load addition or
          modiﬁcation must occur under this Tariﬀ. The Program is composed of two elements: (a) a
          High Impact Load Tariﬀ (“HILT”) and (b) a pro forma High Impact Load Agreement (“HILA”)
          (Appendix A).

   II.     DEFINITIONS AND ACRONYMS

The following deﬁnitions and acronyms apply to the Tariﬀ.


   2.1    Applicable OATT shall mean the Open Access Transmission Tariﬀ governing a transmission
          provider’s rates and non-rate terms and conditions for transmission service, including
          transmission and market administration tariﬀs applicable to the Tri-State Delivery Point which
          serves the Utility Member where the High Impact Load Project will interconnect.

   2.2    Business Day shall mean any day except (a) any Saturday or Sunday, (b) any day which is a legal
          holiday or any day on which banking institutions in Colorado are authorized or required by law
          or other governmental action to close, or (c) any other day that is a Tri-State holiday.

   2.3    Class A Rate shall mean the rate charged by Tri-State to Utility Members for all-requirements
          service pursuant to the WESCs, as accepted by and in eﬀect with FERC.

   2.4    Current High Impact Load Cycle shall mean the High Impact Load Cycle that Tri-State is in the
          process of evaluating.
   2.5    Day shall mean all days, inclusive of weekends and holidays. For clarity, all deadlines will be
          counted exclusive of the start date, i.e. 30 days from August 1 shall not include August 1 in the
        calculation, but would be August 31. If a deadline would fall on a non-Business Day, that
       deadline shall instead be the following Business Day.
2.6    Delivery Point shall mean Tri-State’s delivery point for Utility Member under the WESC that is
       applicable to the High Impact Load Project.
2.7    Eastern Interconnection shall mean one of the three major alternating current power grids
       operating in North America. The Eastern Interconnection generally encompasses the area east
       of the Rocky Mountain states and a portion of northern Texas.
2.8    Expected Operation Date shall mean the date upon which the High Impact Load Project is
       expected to commence operations with its load expected to be at least eighty (80) percent of
       the Expected Project Demand.
2.9    Expected Project Demand shall mean the expected load/demand of the Project as identiﬁed in
       Exhibit A of the HILA.
2.10   Facilities Construction Agreement shall mean the contract between Tri-State and Utility
       Member to construct any required transmission upgrades to serve the High Impact Load. All
       construction costs under the Facilities Construction Agreement shall be paid by the Utility
       Member, per the terms of the Facilities Construction Agreement.
2.11   Facilities Construction Agreement Execution Deadline shall mean the date described in
       Section 6.2.
2.12   Feasibility Study Assessment shall mean the initial evaluation performed by Tri-State during the
       Proposal Planning Period. The Feasibility Study Assessment will be performed at no cost to
       Utility Member, and is required to enter a High Impact Load Cycle. The Feasibility Study
       Assessment is generally modeled on a standard system impact study, and will consider
       alternatives, including a single entity concept analysis and storage alternatives, where
       applicable. Further, the Feasibility Study Assessment will incorporate existing designated
       network loads in the Tri-State queue. Tri-State will use reasonable eﬀorts to complete the
       Feasibility Study Assessments within 90 Days after the meeting with the Utility Member to
       discuss the Member Project Request.
2.13   FERC shall mean the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and any successor organization
       thereto.
2.14   High Impact Load shall mean any load addition located in the Western Interconnection that:
       (1) exceeds 45 MW at the time of the Member Project Request; or (2) is forecasted to exceed
       45 MW within four years from the time of the Member Project Request. High Impact Load
       served under this Tariﬀ shall generally mean a single Tri-State Delivery Point. Aggregation of
       loads under this Tariﬀ shall be limited. Tri-State will aggregate loads that are located within 5
       physical miles of each other and that (1) share one or more of the following: common owner(s),
       a common parent company, common control; and (2) share one or more of the following:
       common local electrical infrastructure, physical layout, character of service, and end use. High
       Impact Load shall not refer to loads that are permanently physically disconnected and
       electrically isolated from any transmission system or transmission system-interconnected
       distribution system and that are incapable of aﬀecting any transmission system or transmission
       system-interconnected distribution system.
2.15   HILA shall mean the High Impact Load Agreement in the form of Appendix A to this Tariﬀ
       between Tri-State and the Utility Member to facilitate the responsibility for serving the High
       Impact Load Project.
 2.16   High Impact Load Customer shall mean the retail customer of the Utility Member related to
       the High Impact Load Project as speciﬁed in the Participation Package.
2.17   High Impact Load Cycle shall mean the two-year cycle, beginning no later than 60 Days after
       FERC acceptance of this Tariﬀ for the ﬁrst High Impact Load Cycle, as further described in
       Section 3.4, and beginning in the third quarter of a calendar year for all future High Impact
       Load Cycles.
2.18   High Impact Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Meeting shall mean the informational meeting Tri-State will hold
       with all Utility Members and interested or potential High Impact Load Customers. The High
       Impact Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Meeting will occur no later than 15 Business Days after the start of a
       new High Impact Load Cycle.
2.19   High Impact Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Notice shall mean the formal notice sent to all Utility Members
       30 Days prior to the launch of a new High Impact Load Cycle. For the ﬁrst High Impact Load
       Cycle, the eﬀective date of this Tariﬀ as established by FERC shall constitute the High Impact
       Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Notice.
2.20   High Impact Load Cycle Planning & Participation Period shall mean the process described in
       Section V.
2.21   High Impact Load Evaluation shall mean the evaluation process described in Sections 5.7, 5.9,
       and 5.10 of this Tariﬀ to determine whether the High Impact Load meets the Program
       Evaluation Criteria.
2.22   High Impact Load Evaluation Fee shall mean the non-refundable fee that Utility Member must
       pay to Tri-State as part of the Participation Package. The High Impact Load Evaluation Fee shall
       be as follows: $35,000 plus $1,000 per MW for Member Project Requests less than 80 MW;
       $150,000 for Member Project Requests between 80 MW and 200 MW; and $250,000 for
       Member Project Requests larger than 200 MW. Tri-State will pool all High Impact Load
       Evaluation Fees during the same High Impact Load Cycle and use them for the cost of the
       Independent Evaluator and for OATT-required studies on a pro rata basis.
2.23   High Impact Load Project shall mean any High Impact Load located in the Western
       Interconnection submitted by a Utility Member to Tri-State under this Tariﬀ.
2.24   Independent Evaluator shall have the meaning described in Section 5.13.
2.25   Member Contract with High Impact Load (“MCHIL”) shall mean the commitment agreement
       between the Utility Member and High Impact Load Customer for the High Impact Load Project.
2.26   Member Project Request shall mean the Tri-State form that Utility Members use to provide
       information regarding High Impact Load Project proposals to Tri-State. Information required
       therein may include High Impact Load Project size, location, Expected Operation Date, term of
       requested service, projected demand, projected monthly energy usage, technology, load
       proﬁle, operational characteristics, and interconnection-related information. If there are
       multiple sub-45 MW loads requesting service located within 5 physical miles of each other, Tri-
       State may request information necessary to determine whether load aggregation is
       appropriate under Section 2.13. A Utility Member may submit a Member Project Request to
       Tri-State at any point to initiate the Proposal Planning Process. A pro forma Member Project
       Request is attached hereto as Appendix B.
2.27   MW shall mean megawatt(s).
2.28   MWh shall mean megawatt-hour(s).
2.29   Network Customer shall have the meaning in the Applicable OATT.
 2.30   Network Integration Transmission Service shall have the meaning in the Applicable OATT.
2.31   Network Resource shall have the meaning in the Applicable OATT.
2.32   Participation Package shall mean all items which a Utility Member must provide to Tri-State to
       participate in the High Impact Load Cycle Planning Process as speciﬁed in Section 5.5.2.
2.33   Participation Requirements shall mean the criteria speciﬁed in Sections IV and V that Utility
       Member must provide to participate in the High Impact Load Program, including the completed
       Participation Package.
2.34   Program Evaluation Criteria shall mean the economic, reliability, and responsibility criteria
       described in Section 5.10.
2.35   Proposal Planning Process shall mean the informational process that must be completed prior
       to entering a High Impact Load Cycle, as described in Section IV. A Utility Member may initiate
       the Proposal Planning Process at any time by submitting a Member Project Request for a High
       Impact Load Project.
2.36   Revised High Impact Load Evaluation Process shall mean the process described in Section 5.8
       used to evaluate High Impact Load Projects that fail the initial High Impact Load Evaluation,
       which is available at the mutually agreed upon option of the Utility Member and High Impact
       Load Customer.
2.37   Security Requirement shall mean those ﬁnal security requirements in Section 7 of the HILA.
2.38   Utility Member shall mean a Tri-State member-owner distribution cooperative or public
       power district with a WESC.
2.39   WESC shall mean the all-requirements wholesale electric service contract between Tri-State
       and Utility Member.
2.40   Western Interconnection shall mean one of the three major alternating current power grids
       operating in North America. The Western Interconnection generally encompasses the Rocky
       Mountain states west to the Paciﬁc Ocean.

III.    HIGH IMPACT LOAD DEVELOPMENT THROUGH THE PROGRAM

3.1    Program. The Program described in this Tariﬀ applies to a Utility Member serving or seeking
       to serve High Impact Load Projects. Such request for service must be done pursuant to the
       terms, conditions, and procedures described herein. Utility Members that seek to add High
       Impact Loads under the Program will do so by submitting a Member Project Request to Tri-
       State, along with other materials required under the Participation Requirements, including the
       completed Participation Package. Subject to passing the Program Evaluation Criteria and
       agreeing to the terms of this Tariﬀ, the Utility Member will enter into a HILA with Tri-State to
       facilitate serving the High Impact Load. Tri-State will model the High Impact Load as part of its
       resource planning and acquisition process and will seek transmission service pursuant to the
       Applicable OATT.
3.2    Proposal Planning Process. This Tariﬀ requires that Tri-State’s Proposal Planning Process must
       be completed prior to a project entering the High Impact Load Cycle (Section IV). The Proposal
       Planning Process will end once a Utility Member has received the ﬁnal Feasibility Study
       Assessment it requests.
3.3    HILA. This Tariﬀ requires that a Utility Member execute a HILA to proceed to the High Impact
       Load Cycle. A pro forma HILA is attached here to as Appendix A, and Utility Member must
          comply with all the terms and conditions contained therein, including the Security
         Requirements.
3.4      High Impact Load Cycles. This Tariﬀ establishes a project evaluation and contracting process
         wherein Tri-State will provide detailed feedback on speciﬁc High Impact Loads submitted by
         Utility Members. This process, referred to herein as a High Impact Load Cycle, will be
         conducted every two years, with the ﬁrst High Impact Load Cycle starting in the year that this
         Tariﬀ is accepted and becomes eﬀective with FERC.
3.5      Overall Availability of Service Under the High Impact Load Program. There is no maximum
         amount of High Impact Load under the High Impact Load Tariﬀ.

IV.      PROPOSAL PLANNING PROCESS
4.1      Proposal Planning Process. A Utility Member may initiate the Proposal Planning Process at any
         time and at no cost by submitting to Tri-State a Member Project Request that Tri-State has
         veriﬁed as complete and accurate. Based on the Member Project Request, during the Proposal
         Planning Process, Tri-State and Utility Member will work collaboratively through the Feasibility
         Study Assessment to identify optimal locations to interconnect the High Impact Load. Tri-State
         will undertake multiple rounds of Feasibility Study Assessments, at Utility Member’s request.
         Tri-State will use reasonable eﬀorts to complete the Feasibility Study Assessment within 90
         Days after the meeting with the Utility Member to discuss the Member Project Request. The
         Feasibility Study Assessment is for informational purposes only, and Utility Member is under
         no obligation to undertake multiple rounds of Feasibility Study Assessments.
      1.1.1. Tri-State will ensure that all pending HIL Feasibility Assessment Studies applicable to the
            Current High Impact Load Cycle are completed prior to Participation Package deadline,
            provided such requests were submitted at least 90 Days prior to said deadline.
4.2 Aggregation. As part of the Proposal Planning Process, Tri-State will aggregate multiple loads into
    a single High Impact Load Project consistent with the deﬁnition of High Impact Load based on the
    information provided in the Member Project Request.

V.        HIGH IMPACT LOAD CYCLE PLANNING PROCESS

5.1      Schedules for the First and Subsequent High Impact Load Cycles. To allow for timely
         implementation, the ﬁrst High Impact Load Cycle will follow the “First High Impact Load Cycle”
         deadlines and time periods provided in Schedule 1 to this Tariﬀ, notwithstanding any other
         provision of this Tariﬀ to the contrary. All subsequent High Impact Load Cycles will follow the
         deadlines and time periods described in the body of this Tariﬀ and summarized in Schedule 1
         under “Subsequent High Impact Load Cycles.” The ﬁrst High Impact Load Cycle will begin 60
         Days after the eﬀective date of the Tariﬀ established by FERC. Subsequent High Impact Load
         Cycles will commence every fall, two years after the ﬁrst High Impact Load Cycle, 30 Days after
         issuance of a High Impact Load Kickoﬀ Notice.
5.2      High Impact Load Kickoﬀ Meeting. No later than 15 Business Days after the start of the High
         Impact Load Cycle, Tri-State will hold an informational High Impact Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Meeting
         regarding the Current High Impact Load Cycle available to all Utility Members and to all their
         interested or potential High Impact Load Customers. Tri-State will send notice of the High
         Impact Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Meeting to all Utility Members. Utility Members will be responsible
         for providing notice to their High Impact Load Customers. During the High Impact Load Cycle
         Kickoﬀ Meeting, Tri-State will outline the timing and steps of the Current High Impact Load
          Cycle, provide Participation Package requirements, and be available to answer any Utility
         Member questions.
5.3      HILA. Utility Member will execute a HILA as part of the Participation Package within 30 Days
         of the High Impact Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Meeting. Tri-State will promptly countersign the HILA
         and return a fully executed HILA to Utility Member once the High Impact Load Project passes
         the evaluation process described below.
      5.3.1.Tri-State plans to use the pro forma HILA ﬁled with and accepted by FERC, and will not ﬁle
            such conforming HILAs at FERC. To the extent that a non-conforming HILA is executed, or
            FERC directs otherwise, Tri-State will ﬁle the HILA with FERC within 60 Days after the High
            Impact Load Project passes the evaluation process described below.
5.4      High Impact Load Evaluation Process. Once the Current High Impact Load Cycle has begun, Tri-
         State will promptly begin evaluating all High Impact Load Projects participating in that Cycle
         that meet the Tariﬀ’s requirements pursuant to the requirements of this Section.
5.5      Participation Package Contents, Veriﬁcation, and Deadlines
      5.5.1.Submission Deadline. Within 30 Days of the High Impact Load Cycle Kickoﬀ Meeting, Utility
            Member will submit to Tri-State a complete Participation Package.
      5.5.2.Contents. The Participation Package will include the following: (a) a completed Member
            Project Request; (b) a High Impact Load Evaluation Fee; (c) an executed MCHIL; and (d) an
            executed HILA.
            5.5.2.1. Aggregation. The following Participation Package requirements will apply if Tri-
                    State aggregates loads for a single Utility Member or across multiple Utility
                    Members’ service territories. In these instances, Tri-State will coordinate with Utility
                    Member(s) to revise the Member Project Request, and such revisions will not be
                    deemed to delay eligibility to participate in the current High Impact Load Cycle. If
                    across multiple Utility Members’ service territories, the Utility Members will
                    coordinate to submit a single Participation Package, and must nominate a Utility
                    Member to be the point of contact for this HILT process.
              5.5.2.1.1.       A completed Member Project Request for each load;
              5.5.2.1.2.      Each Utility Member shall be responsible for the High Impact Load
                       Evaluation Fee on a pro rata basis, based on the percentage of the total High
                       Impact Load located within each of their respective service territories, unless
                       they agree otherwise;
              5.5.2.1.3.       An executed MCHIL for each load; and,
              5.5.2.1.4.       An executed HILA for each Utility Member for all load aggregated for
                       that Utility Member.
      5.5.3.Veriﬁcation. Within 20 Business Days of the receipt of the Participation Package, Tri-State
            will complete its veriﬁcation of Participation Package for accuracy and completeness and
            provide Utility Member with notice if the Participation Package is deemed complete or
            stating any deﬁciencies.
            5.5.3.1. For High Impact Load Projects that fail the veriﬁcation process, Utility Member
                    will have 10 Business Days to cure any defects identiﬁed in its Participation Package.
              5.5.3.1.1.      A Utility Member that fails to submit a cured Participation Package will be
                       deemed to have its High Impact Load Project withdrawn from the current High
                       Impact Load Cycle.
             5.5.3.2. Within 5 Business Days of the receipt of a revised Participation Package, Tri-State
                    will complete its veriﬁcation of the revised Participation Package for accuracy and
                    completeness and provide Utility Member with notice if the Participation Package is
                    deemed complete or if there are any uncured deﬁciencies.
            5.5.3.3. High Impact Load Projects that pass either stage of the veriﬁcation process will
                    proceed to the High Impact Load Evaluation.
            5.5.3.4. By mutual agreement, Tri-State and Utility Member may extend any of the
                    deadlines in Section 5.5.3 by up to 5 Business Days to cure administrative errors.
            5.5.3.5. High Impact Load Projects that fail both stages of the veriﬁcation process will be
                    deemed withdrawn from the Current High Impact Load Cycle, without prejudice to
                    the Utility Member resubmitting the High Impact Load Project during a subsequent
                    High Impact Load Program Cycle.
5.6      MCHIL Requirements. As part of the Participation Package, Utility Member must submit a
         fully executed MCHIL. Tri-State is not responsible for compliance with any terms or
         conditions of a Utility Member’s agreements with third parties.
5.7      Evaluation Process for Initial Proposal Period. No later than 150 Days from the start of the
         Current High Impact Load Cycle, Tri-State will complete the evaluation of all valid High Impact
         Load Projects and will provide to Utility Members that submitted a validated Participation
         Package notice of the results of the evaluation of that Utility Member’s High Impact Load
         Project, including an analysis of the characteristics that led to acceptance or rejection.

      5.7.1.Tri-State may request additional information not identiﬁed in the Participation Package but
            reasonably necessary for the evaluation of a High Impact Load during the Initial Proposal
            Period. Utility Members are solely responsible for meeting the submission deadline and
            ensuring the submittal of complete and accurate information, provided that Tri-State may
            allow for the correction of any deﬁciencies, where doing so will not materially impact the
            evaluation process, in terms of delay, additional costs, or otherwise.

5.8      Revised Proposal Period. If there are High Impact Load Projects that were not accepted under
         the evaluation process described above in Section 5.7, a Revised Proposal Process will be
         initiated. The Revised Proposal Process will start on the ﬁrst Business Day after the Initial
         Proposal Period ends and will last for 20 Business Days. If no High Impact Load Project fails the
         evaluation during the Initial Proposal Period, or if all Utility Members participating in the
         Current High Impact Load Cycle who were not accepted during the Initial Proposal Period
         inform Tri-State in writing that they do not intend to submit a revised Participation Package,
         the Revised Proposal Period and evaluation under this Section will be skipped.
         5.8.1. Within 5 Business Days of the start of the Revised Proposal Period, Tri-State will meet
                with the applicable Utility Member(s) to review the results for High Impact Load
                Project(s) that failed the evaluation and discuss modiﬁcations to those Participation
                Package(s) that could make the High Impact Project more likely to succeed. Discussions
                during these meetings do not constitute acceptance of High Impact Load Project, which
                can only be achieved through passing the evaluation process.

         5.8.2. The Utility Member will have 10 Business Days from its meeting with Tri-State to submit
                a revised Participation Package to trigger reevaluation. Revisions can include material
                changes, including but not limited to: High Impact Load Project size, minimum demand
                threshold, location, and load ramp. An additional High Impact Load Evaluation Fee will
                not apply to a revised Participation Package. The revised High Impact Load Project will
               be subject to the same requirements in Section 5.10 as other High Impact Load Project
              submitted under Section 5.7. If no Revised High Impact Load Projects are submitted
              within the Revised Proposal Period, the remainder of the Revised Proposal Period will
              be skipped.

       5.8.3. Tri-State may request additional information not identiﬁed in the revised Participation
              Package but reasonably necessary for the evaluation of a High Impact Load during the
              Revised Proposal Period. Utility Members are solely responsible for meeting the
              submission deadline and ensuring the submittal of complete and accurate information,
              provided that Tri-State may allow for the correction of any deﬁciencies, where doing so
              will not materially impact the evaluation process, in terms of delay, additional costs, or
              otherwise.

       5.8.4. No later than the last Business Day of the Revised Proposal Period, Tri-State will
              complete the evaluation of all revised Participation Packages and will provide to Utility
              Members that submitted a revised Participation Package during the Revised Proposal
              Period notice of the results of the evaluation of that Utility Member’s revised High
              Impact Load Project, including an analysis of the characteristics that led to acceptance
              or rejection.

5.9    Evaluation Methodology for High Impact Load Projects. Tri-State will evaluate High Impact Load
       Projects using the same commercially available resource planning software in use at Tri-State
       at the time of that High Impact Load Program Cycle.
       5.9.1. Tri-State will use the software to assess bulk power system and market characteristics,
              as well as the price and non-price characteristics of submitted High Impact Load
              Projects, in determining whether the criteria in Section 5.10 have been satisﬁed. For a
              high impact load evaluation, the model would be informed by: (a) the size, timing, and
              location of load; (b) the size, timing, cost and location of available generic resources to
              be built or procured; and (c) the applicable environmental, reliability, and transmission
              constraints.

5.10   Evaluation Criteria. Tri-State will evaluate High Impact Load Projects using the four criteria set
       forth below. Absent a relevant change in law or regulation, the evaluation criteria will comport,
       as appropriate, with the metrics and standards applied by Tri-State in its most recent resource
       planning process or Bring Your Own Resource Tariﬀ cycle and will not be altered or otherwise
       diverge for purposes of High Impact Load Program evaluation, though the High Impact Load
       Evaluation may utilize more recent data inputs, as appropriate. An Independent Evaluator will
       review and conﬁrm that Tri-State’s High Impact Load Evaluation Process was conducted
       consistently with the terms of this Tariﬀ. Tri-State will make all evaluations consistent with the
       WESC’s requirement to use Good Utility Practice to serve Utility Member load.
       5.10.1. Reliability Criteria. The evaluation will consider whether the High Impact Load Project
               has an adverse impact on the reliable operation of the Tri-State system as measured by
               reliability metrics identiﬁed in Tri-State’s resource planning processes, along with any
               other reliability or regulatory requirements that may apply. Only High Impact Load
               Projects which are determined to allow Tri-State to continue to achieve the reliability
               metrics will pass evaluation.

              Tri-State utilizes two levels of reliability metrics in all resource plan modeling to ensure
              a reliable system:
       5.10.1.1. Level 1 Reliability Metrics: Include a planning reserve margin and eﬀective load
             carrying capability ratings by technology, based on stochastic modeling of Tri-State’s
             system and region to determine a reliability level that does not exceed more than
             one day of load loss in 10 years.

      5.10.1.2. Level 2 Reliability Metrics: A set of metrics speciﬁc to evaluating system
             performance in simulated extreme weather event conditions for summer and winter
             seasons that considers stresses on load, resources, market pricing and availability,
             and transmission availability.

   5.10.2. Economic Criteria. The evaluation will consider whether the new generation and
           transmission resource(s) required to serve the High Impact Load Project will cause cost-
           shifts among Utility Members by analyzing whether the High Impact Load Project, and
           additional associated resources, increases Tri-State’s member rate over the term of the
           High Impact Load Project as compared to Tri-State’s Class A Rate in eﬀect on the ﬁrst
           day of the High Impact Load Cycle. Such analysis will consider the cost of transmission
           upgrades and additional production capacity required to serve the High Impact Load
           Project as well as the increase in Tri-State’s system peak load and annual energy demand
           based on the High Impact Load Project’s minimum demand and energy amounts. Only
           High Impact Load Projects that would not be directly responsible for an increase to Tri-
           State’s member rate over the term of the High Impact Load Project as compared to Tri-
           State’s Class A Rate in eﬀect on the ﬁrst day of the High Impact Load Cycle will pass the
           evaluation.

   5.10.3. Environmental Criteria. The evaluation will consider whether the High Impact Load
           Project adversely impacts Tri-State’s compliance with: (a) Tri-State's board-approved
           environmental goals and (b) mandated greenhouse gas reduction targets, renewable
           energy procurement obligations, or other environmental requirements as established
           by applicable regulatory authorities. Only High Impact Load Projects which are
           determined to allow Tri-State to continue to achieve compliance with: (a) Tri-State's
           environmental goals and (b) mandated greenhouse gas reduction targets, renewable
           energy procurement obligations, or other environmental requirements as established
           by applicable regulatory authorities will pass the evaluation.
   5.10.4. Transmission metrics. The evaluation will consider whether the timing of necessary
           transmission upgrades to meet the High Impact Load Project’s Expected Operation
           Date is feasible. Only High Impact Load Projects where it is determined to be feasible
           to timely make necessary transmission upgrades to meet the High Impact Load
           Project’s Expected Operation Date will pass the evaluation.
5.10.5. Competing Loads Ranking. In the event that two or more High Impact Load Projects in the
      same general location would result in a failure of one or more Evaluation Criteria, but would
      otherwise succeed individually, Tri-State will rank those High Impact Load Projects based on
      their results under the Economic Criteria. The Independent Evaluator will conﬁrm this
      ranking. Only the High Impact Load Project(s) which are most economical will proceed.
       5.10.5.1. Pro-Rating. Alternatively, Utility Members whose High Impact Load Projects were
              subject to a competing loads ranking may mutually agree to pro rate their High
              Impact Load Projects by modifying their High Impact Load Projects so that they
              would pass all Evaluation Criteria. If the Utility Members are unable to mutually
              agree on how to pro rate their High Impact Load Projects within 10 Business Days,
              Tri-State will move forward with the most economical High Impact Load Projects as
              described in Section 5.10.5.
 5.11      High Impact Load Projects that Fail Evaluation. A High Impact Load Project that fails evaluation
          under Section 5.10 or any other provision of this Tariﬀ will not result in a ﬁnancial penalty to
          the relevant Utility Member, and will be without prejudice to the Utility Member resubmitting
          the High Impact Load Project during a subsequent High Impact Load Program Cycle.
5.12      Expected Operation Date. The Utility Member must identify an Expected Operation Date in its
          Member Project Request that, after a High Impact Load Project is accepted, may only be
          changed as provided by the HILA.
5.13      Independent Evaluator. Tri-State will retain an Independent Evaluator to review whether Tri-
          State’s High Impact Load Evaluation Process was conducted consistently with the terms of this
          Tariﬀ, including any ranking that may occur under the Economic Criteria.
       5.13.1. Tri-State will request that the Independent Evaluator use reasonable eﬀorts to complete
             its review 15 Business Days from the later of the end of the Proposal Period or the Revised
             Proposal Period (if applicable). Independent Evaluator will notify Tri-State of the results of
             its review, subject to applicable conﬁdentiality agreements described in Section 7.1. After
             Tri-State and the Independent Evaluator mutually agree that the review is complete and
             accurate, Tri-State will promptly forward such results to all Utility Members.

VI.        HIGH IMPACT LOAD TRANSMISSION PROCESS

6.1.      Transmission Service. All transmission service, requests, planning, and other related processes
          will take place under the Applicable OATT. Nothing in this Tariﬀ is intended to otherwise aﬀect
          rights under the Applicable OATT.

6.2.      Facilities Construction Agreement. Utility Member must execute a Facilities Construction
          Agreement requiring that Utility Member be responsible for costs of all interconnection
          facilities and upgrades directly assigned to Tri-State, except for those Network Upgrades under
          SPP’s Attachment AX, necessary to serve the High Impact Load, and provide appropriate
          security for such interconnection facilities and upgrades prior to the execution of Applicable
          OATT study agreement, unless otherwise mutually agreed to. In the event that loads are
          aggregated, applicable costs directly assigned to Tri-State will be allocated among each
          respective aggregated Utility Member on a pro rata basis. Tri-State will ﬁle at FERC the executed
          Facilities Construction Agreement within 15 Business Days of receipt of an executed Facilities
          Construction Agreement from Utility Member. If Tri-State and Utility Member cannot come to
          an agreement, Tri-State will instead ﬁle an unexecuted Facilities Construction Agreement with
          FERC.

VII.       CONFIDENTIALITY AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION

7.1.      Conﬁdentiality Agreements. Upon request of the Utility Member or Tri-State to protect the
          conﬁdential information and data of Tri-State, Utility Member, and its High Impact Load
          Customer, Tri-State, Independent Evaluator, and as applicable, Utility Member and its High
          Impact Load Customer, will execute a standard conﬁdentiality agreement that provides for the
          conﬁdential treatment of commercially sensitive information. Notwithstanding the foregoing,
          Tri-State may disclose any conﬁdential information and data to applicable third parties,
          including regulatory or judicial authorities, in connection with any transmission service,
          requests, planning, and other processes that will take place under the Applicable OATT and this
          Tariﬀ.
 7.2.   Dispute Resolution. Any Utility Member that disputes how a High Impact Load Cycle was
       conducted, or the outcome of a High Impact Load Cycle, may ﬁle a complaint with FERC. Utility
       Member must ﬁrst avail themselves of the Dispute Resolutions procedures contained in the
       HILA, to the extent the dispute is related to the scope of the HILA.
